pos: n. (a composition to be sung; the sung praise of God; rendering Hebrew shir, Greek ode)
etymology: From the Saxon sang, from singan, to sing. Hebrew shir is both the song and the singing of it; the Psalter's titles preserve the distinction between a mizmor (psalm, set to instruments) and a shir (song).
biblical_def: The first song in Scripture is sung on the far shore of a drowned army: “Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD… I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously” (Exodus 15:1). That sets the pattern for everything after it — biblical song is response to a completed act of God, not a means of working one up. The Psalter repeatedly speaks of a new song given after deliverance: “he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God” (Psalm 40:3), and the effect named there is evangelistic, for many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD. Song is put in the mouth by God and works outward on the hearers. In heaven the redeemed sing a new song whose lyric is stated: “Thou art worthy… for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood” (Revelation 5:9). The subject is the atonement, and the singers are those it purchased. Paul makes singing a means of the word's indwelling rather than an ornament attached to it: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly… teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3:16). Congregational singing is there described as a teaching ministry that every member exercises toward every other — which is why what a church sings is a doctrinal question before it is a musical one.
webster_summary: A composition to be sung. Scripture makes it response to God's finished acts, gives its heavenly lyric as the atonement, and calls congregational singing a means of teaching one another the word of Christ.
webster_full: SONG, n. [Sax. sang, from singan, to sing.] In general, that which is sung or uttered with musical modulations of the voice.
2. A little poem to be sung, or set to music.
3. A hymn; a sacred poem or hymn designed to be sung in the worship of God.
4. A lay; a strain; the notes of birds.
5. Old song, a trifle; as, I would not buy it for an old song.
corruption_summary: Congregational song is treated as a warm-up for the sermon or as a device for producing feeling, rather than as the teaching and admonishing ministry Colossians 3:16 says it is.
corruption_paragraphs: Where singing is understood chiefly as atmosphere, two things follow quickly. The lyric stops being examined for doctrine, because nobody audits a mood; and the congregation stops being the choir, because a mood is more efficiently produced by a platform. Colossians 3:16 resists both. It says the word of Christ dwells in a people as they teach and admonish one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. That makes every line sung a line taught, and makes the man in the fourth row a teacher of his neighbour whether he can carry a tune or not. A church that would never tolerate an untrue sentence from the pulpit, but sings whatever is current, has not grasped that it is being catechised either way.

The principle to recover is that song follows an accomplished work. Israel sang after the sea was crossed, not to get it to part; the Psalmist receives a new song because he has been lifted out of the miry clay; the redeemed in Revelation sing because a Lamb was slain. This ordering protects worship from becoming a technique. The regulative principle of worship applies here as everywhere — what God has commanded is required and what he has not commanded is not permitted — and the Psalter remains the church's inspired songbook and the standard by which her other songs are measured.
roots_summary: Hebrew shir is a song or the act of singing; mizmor is a psalm set to instrumental accompaniment. Greek ode is a song, and psalmos a psalm.
roots_lines: Hebrew shir (H7892) — a song; also the singing of it, as in the Song of songs.
Hebrew mizmor (H4210) — a psalm, a song set to instrumental music; the heading of many Psalms.
Hebrew zamar (H2167) — to make music, to sing praise with accompaniment.
Greek ode (G5603) — a song, an ode; the word in spiritual songs, Colossians 3:16.
Greek humnos (G5215) — a hymn, a song of praise addressed to God.
usage: Of song as response to deliverance: then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD (Exodus 15:1).
Of the new song given after rescue: he hath put a new song in my mouth (Psalm 40:3).
Of singing as a teaching ministry: teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Colossians 3:16).

pos: n. pl. (those appointed to sing in the worship of God; rendering Hebrew sharim, from shir)
etymology: From sing, Saxon singan. In the Old Testament the word is chiefly an office-title rather than a description of ability: the singers are a named order of Levites, enrolled by family and paid out of the temple revenues.
biblical_def: In Israel the singers were an order, not a talent pool. David appointed them, and the Chronicler lists them by house: “The singers: the children of Asaph, an hundred twenty and eight” (Ezra 2:41) — counted in the return from Babylon alongside priests and porters, because the service of song was part of the fabric of the house of God. Nehemiah traces the arrangement to its author: “For in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving unto God” (Nehemiah 12:46). The Psalter shows them in procession: “The singers went before, the players on instruments followed after” (Psalm 68:25). And at the dedication of Solomon's temple their unity is the hinge on which the glory turns: “as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD… then the house was filled with a cloud” (2 Chronicles 5:13). The text dwells on as one and one sound. What God honoured was not virtuosity but unity in a common confession — and the words they sang are given: for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever. The singers were, in effect, an order of preachers with a tune.
webster_summary: Those appointed to sing in God's worship — in Israel a Levitical order enrolled by family. At the temple's dedication their unity in one confession, not their skill, is what the glory answers.
webster_full: SINGER, n. One that sings; one skilled in music, or whose occupation is to sing.
2. One whose office it is to sing in public worship; as the singers appointed by David.
3. A bird that sings; a songster.
4. SINGING, ppr. Uttering melodious or musical notes; celebrating in song.
5. In Scripture, the singers were a distinct order of the Levites, 1 Chron. 15.
corruption_summary: The singers become performers and the congregation an audience, so that a service is judged as a concert is judged and the people's own voice grows quiet.
corruption_paragraphs: The Levitical singers led a singing people; they did not replace them. The danger in every age is that the appointed voices grow loud enough to make the congregation optional, and the marks of it are familiar — lighting arranged for a platform, volume that covers the room, keys pitched for a soloist, and songs whose lines a normal man cannot follow at first hearing. Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 both address the whole church, not a section of it. Where the people cannot hear themselves, the ministry those verses describe has been quietly transferred to a few, and the many have been reduced to appreciating it.

The principle to recover is the one the Chronicler underlines at the dedication: the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound. The glory did not descend on excellence; it descended on unity in a true confession of God's goodness and mercy. That is a standard any congregation can meet and no amount of skill can substitute for. It also sets the right ambition for those who lead: not to be heard, but to get a whole house saying the same true thing at the same moment.
roots_summary: Hebrew shir (to sing) gives the participle sharim, the singers; the Chronicler treats them as a Levitical order alongside porters and priests.
roots_lines: Hebrew shir (H7891) — to sing; the participle gives the singers as an office.
Hebrew Leviyyim (H3881) — Levites; the tribe from which the singers were drawn.

Hebrew menatstseach (H5329) — the chief Musician, the overseer named in many Psalm titles.
Greek ado (G103) — to sing; used of the singing of the church and of the redeemed in heaven.

Of the order's origin: in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers (Nehemiah 12:46).

pos: n. and v. (that which is heard; a noise, tone, or report; rendering Hebrew qol, Greek phone and echos)
etymology: From the Latin sonus, through Old French son. The English word also carries a wholly separate line from the Saxon gesund, whole or healthy — which is the sound of sound doctrine, a homonym rather than a metaphor, though the coincidence has served preachers well.
biblical_def: Sound in Scripture is what reaches the ear, and the Bible is repeatedly interested in whether it is intelligible. Paul's rule for the assembly turns on it: “if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?” (1 Corinthians 14:8). A trumpet was a code, not a noise — particular calls meant advance, retreat, assemble — so an indistinct blast was worse than silence. That is Paul's argument against unintelligible speech in the congregation: sound without meaning does not merely fail to help, it disarms the hearer. The Psalter blesses those who can read the signal: “Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound” (Psalm 89:15), which is the trumpet of the appointed feasts and, beyond it, the gospel it prefigured. Our Lord uses sound for the evidence of an unseen cause: “thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh… so is every one that is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8). The new birth is undetectable in its origin and unmistakable in its effect — you cannot watch the wind, but you can hear it. And Paul takes the psalm of the heavens declaring God's glory and applies it to preaching: “their sound went into all the earth” (Romans 10:18).
webster_summary: That which is heard. Scripture cares that it be intelligible — an uncertain trumpet disarms the soldier — and uses sound for the audible evidence of an unseen work, as of the wind and the new birth.
webster_full: SOUND, n. [L. sonus.] Noise; report; the object of hearing; that which strikes the ear.
2. A vibration of the air, produced by a body in motion, and perceived by the organ of hearing.
3. Report; as, the sound of a name went abroad.
4. SOUND, a. [Sax. gesund.] Entire; unbroken; not shaky or defective; as sound timber; healthy; not diseased.
5. Hence, right; correct; well founded; free from error; orthodox; as sound doctrine, 2 Tim. 1.
corruption_summary: Sound is prized for its effect apart from its content, so that music and volume are asked to do what meaning must do — the very uncertain trumpet Paul forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 14 is the plainest chapter in the New Testament on this, and it is routinely read as if it were only about tongues. Its principle is broader: in the assembly, sound exists to convey meaning, and any sound that does not is to be regulated. Paul is willing to sound rude about it — five words with understanding are worth ten thousand in an unknown tongue (1 Corinthians 14:19). Wherever a service is arranged so that the impression outruns the content, the trumpet has grown uncertain, however skilfully it is blown. The test Paul supplies is practical and severe: could an unlearned man who wandered in tell what was being said, and be convinced by it (1 Corinthians 14:24-25)?

The principle to recover is that God has attached his saving work to intelligible sound. Romans 10 makes hearing the ordinary road to faith, and the sound that goes into all the earth is preaching with content in it. This is also the standing answer to the modern claim that new apostles and prophets are speaking today: the canon is closed, and the sound the church is to heed is the one already given. A church that wants power should want clarity, because the Spirit has bound himself to the word preached and not to the volume it is preached at.
roots_summary: Hebrew qol is voice or sound, from thunder to a whisper. Greek phone is voice or sound with meaning; echos is a noise or roar; hugiaino gives the unrelated sound of sound doctrine.
roots_lines: Hebrew qol (H6963) — voice, sound, noise; used of thunder, of trumpets, and of the still small voice.
Hebrew teruah (H8643) — a shout or blast of alarm; the joyful sound of Psalm 89:15.
Greek phone (G5456) — voice, sound; the word behind Romans 10:18 and John 3:8.
Greek echos (G2279) — a roar or noise; the rushing mighty wind of Pentecost.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be healthy, whole; the separate root of sound doctrine.
usage: Of intelligibility in the assembly: if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? (1 Corinthians 14:8).
Of the blessing of knowing the signal: blessed is the people that know the joyful sound (Psalm 89:15).
Of the evidence of an unseen work: thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh (John 3:8).

Psalm 89:15

pos: n. (a loud or confused sound; clamour; rendering Hebrew qol, hamon, and shaon)
etymology: From Old French noise, quarrel or uproar, probably from the Latin nausea by way of the din of a seasick ship's company — a disputed derivation, but the sense of confused and unwelcome sound is ancient in the word.
biblical_def: Noise is sound without discernible sense, and Scripture handles it with a striking evenhandedness. It can be misread: coming down from the mount, “when Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said unto Moses, There is a noise of war in the camp” (Exodus 32:17). It was not war; it was idolatry, which from a distance sounds much the same. It can be genuinely indistinguishable: at the laying of the second temple's foundation, “the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people” (Ezra 3:13) — the young rejoicing and the old men who remembered the first house wept, and the two made one sound. Few verses describe the mingled state of God's people in this world so exactly. It is also what God silences: he “stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people” (Psalm 65:7), the three set side by side because the roaring of the nations is no harder for him than the roaring of the surf. Most soberly, worship itself can become noise in God's ears when the life behind it is corrupt: “Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols” (Amos 5:23). What Israel called music, God called racket.
webster_summary: Loud or confused sound. Scripture shows it misread, shows joy and grief making one indistinguishable noise, shows God stilling it — and warns that unfaithful worship reaches him only as noise.
webster_full: NOISE, n. noiz. [Fr. noise, a quarrel.] Sound of any kind, or proceeding from any cause; but chiefly, loud, confused, or stunning sound.
2. Outcry; clamor; loud complaint or importunity.
3. Frequent talk; much public conversation; as, to make a noise in the world.
4. NOISE, v.i. To sound loud; to make an outcry.
5. NOISE, v.t. To spread by rumor or report; as, it was noised abroad that he was come.
corruption_summary: Amos 5:23 is the standing rebuke to worship offered by an unjust people, yet it is seldom preached — while a general appetite for loudness makes it harder than ever to distinguish sound from noise.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos is speaking to a people whose services were full and whose scales were false. Into that setting God says he hates their feast days, will not smell in their solemn assemblies, and wants the noise of their songs taken away — and then names what he does want: judgment running down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream (Amos 5:24). The passage is not a criticism of music; it is a verdict on worship detached from obedience. It should be preached wherever a congregation is more careful about its sound than about its dealings. God is not obliged to receive as praise what a corrupt life offers him, and he says so in the plainest terms available.

The principle to recover is Ezra 3:13 — that in this world the joy and the grief of God's people are often one sound, and that God hears both accurately even when the bystanders cannot tell them apart. The men who wept had seen the first house; the men who shouted had only ever heard of it. Both responses were right. A congregation containing the elderly who remember better days and the young who are glad of what they have is not divided; it is normal, and the noise it makes together is heard in heaven as two distinct things.
roots_summary: Hebrew qol is sound or voice generally; hamon is a multitude and the roar it makes; shaon is a crash or uproar, used of the seas and of war.
roots_lines: Hebrew qol (H6963) — voice, sound, noise; the general word, judged by context.
Hebrew hamon (H1995) — a multitude, and the tumult it makes; the noise of many peoples.
Hebrew shaon (H7588) — a crash, roar, uproar; the noise of the seas in Psalm 65:7.
Hebrew teruah (H8643) — a shout, alarm, or blast; the shout of joy in Ezra 3.
Greek thorubos (G2351) — an uproar, tumult, disorderly noise of a crowd.

Of joy and grief indistinguishable: could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping (Ezra 3:13).
Of worship rejected as mere noise: take thou away from me the noise of thy songs (Amos 5:23).

Amos 5:23

pos: n. pl. (tools; means by which something is effected; musical instruments; rendering Hebrew keli, Greek hoplon)
etymology: From the Latin instrumentum, a tool or implement, from instruo, to build up, to furnish. The word never names an agent, only a means — which is exactly the point Paul presses in Romans 6.
biblical_def: Instruments in the Authorized Version covers tools of every kind, and two uses matter most. The first is musical, and it is authorised by David's own arrangement: “the Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets” (2 Chronicles 29:26), and again, “four thousand praised the LORD with the instruments which I made, said David, to praise therewith” (1 Chronicles 23:5). The Psalter closes by calling for them by name (Psalm 150:4). But Amos shows the same instruments in the hands of the careless rich, who “chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David” (Amos 6:5) — the comparison to David is the sting. It is possible to imitate David's music while being nothing like David. The second use is moral, and it is the more important. Paul writes: “Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God… and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God” (Romans 6:13). Hands, eyes, and tongue are tools, and a tool serves whoever holds it. The believer is not told to destroy his members but to hand them to a new owner. Sanctification, in Paul's figure, is a transfer of instruments.
webster_summary: Tools; the means by which a thing is done. Scripture uses them for the music of God's house and, in Romans 6, for the members of the body — tools that serve whoever holds them, and are to be handed to God.
webster_full: INSTRUMENT, n. [L. instrumentum, from instruo, to prepare.] A tool; that by which work is performed, or any thing is effected.
2. That which is subservient to the execution of a plan or purpose; a means.
3. An artificial machine or body for producing musical sounds; as an instrument of ten strings.
4. A person who is subservient to another; as, he was the instrument of another's designs.
5. In law, a writing containing a contract, or serving as evidence of a fact.
corruption_summary: The body is treated either as the self, so that its appetites are simply who a man is, or as an enemy to be punished. Romans 6 calls it neither: a set of instruments, to be yielded.
corruption_paragraphs: Two ancient errors return in modern dress. The first identifies a man with his desires, so that what the members want defines what the person is, and refusing an appetite becomes a species of self-denial in the worst sense — a denial of the true self. The second, older and more religious, treats the body as the problem and mortification as a war on flesh and blood, which is not Christian but a relic of the Greek contempt for matter. Paul stands between them with a workman's image. Your members are instruments: not your identity and not your enemy, but tools, morally neutral in themselves and decisive in their use, since a hand can be lifted to bless or to strike.

The principle to recover is that yielding is an act, and a repeatable one. Romans 6:13 is in the imperative, addressed to people already dead to sin and alive to God — the standing of verse 11 comes first, and the yielding of verse 13 follows from it. This is the Reformed order in miniature: because you are in Christ, present your members to God. Sanctification is not the effort by which a man becomes accepted, but the daily handing over of tools by a man already accepted, and it is progressive precisely because there are many instruments and each morning brings them back into his hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew keli is a vessel, tool, weapon, or instrument — anything made for a use. Greek hoplon is a tool or weapon, and gives Romans 6 its military edge.
roots_lines: Hebrew keli (H3627) — a vessel, implement, weapon, or musical instrument; anything fashioned for use.
Hebrew nebel (H5035) — a skin-bottle, and hence a psaltery or lute of similar shape.
Hebrew kinnor (H3658) — the harp or lyre, the instrument of David.
Greek hoplon (G3696) — a tool, implement, or weapon; the word rendered instruments in Romans 6:13.
Greek melos (G3196) — a member or limb of the body; the thing yielded in Romans 6:13.

pos: n. and v. (a loud cry of triumph, alarm, or joy; rendering Hebrew teruah and rua, Greek keleusma)
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps related to scout and to Old Norse skuta, a taunt. In the KJV it consistently renders words for a corporate cry — the sound a whole people makes at once, not an individual's exclamation.
biblical_def: The shout in Scripture is nearly always corporate and nearly always a response to God's act rather than an attempt to produce one. At Jericho the wall does not fall to a battering ram: “the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat” (Joshua 6:20). The shout came after seven days of silent circuits and at a commanded moment; it was obedience made audible, and the victory was God's. At the laying of the second temple's foundation the same word appears: “all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid” (Ezra 3:11) — and again the shout follows a completed work, this time only a foundation, which is instructive. The Psalter commands it as worship: “O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph” (Psalm 47:1). And the New Testament reserves one shout for the end: “the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). The Greek there is keleusma, a commander's order shouted to troops or rowers. The last shout of history is not a cheer from the church but a word of command from her Lord, and the dead obey it.
webster_summary: A loud corporate cry. In Scripture it follows God's finished work — Jericho fallen, a foundation laid — and the final shout is not the church's cheer but her Lord's word of command, at which the dead rise.
webster_full: SHOUT, v.i. To utter a sudden and loud outcry, usually in joy, triumph or exultation.
2. To utter a loud cry as of alarm or in battle.
3. SHOUT, n. A loud burst of voice or voices; a vehement and sudden outcry, particularly of a multitude expressing joy, triumph, exultation or animated courage.
4. A cry of alarm or of onset in battle.
5. In Scripture, the shout of a king is among them, Num. 23; the people shouted with a great shout, Josh. 6.
corruption_summary: The shout is treated as a technique for generating spiritual power, especially where modern apostles and prophets promise breakthrough by volume, when Scripture makes it a response to what God has already done.
corruption_paragraphs: The New Apostolic Reformation and the wider charismatic movements have made a good deal of the shout of Jericho, teaching that a decreed or shouted word can pull down strongholds in a believer's circumstances. The narrative will not support it. Israel's shout was on the seventh day, at a commanded moment, after six days of enforced silence, and the wall fell because God had already given the city (Joshua 6:2, spoken before a single circuit). The shout did not produce the victory; it obeyed a command about a victory already granted. Treating it as a technique reverses the order and puts the power in the mouth of the shouter — which is why such teaching so reliably ends in the disappointment of ordinary people who shouted and saw nothing fall.

The principle to recover is the direction of the last shout. In 1 Thessalonians 4:16 the shout comes down, not up: it is keleusma, the word an officer gives, and the response is not louder praise but resurrection. Every corporate shout in Scripture is a rehearsal of that one. The church's hope is not in what she can raise but in what he will speak, and the dead in Christ, who cannot shout at all, will be the first to answer it.
roots_summary: Hebrew teruah is a shout or blast, of alarm or of joy; rua is the verb, to raise a shout. Greek keleusma is a shouted command, used only once, of Christ's descent.
roots_lines: Hebrew teruah (H8643) — a shout, an alarm, a blast; the noun at Jericho and at the feasts.
Hebrew rua (H7321) — to raise a shout, to sound an alarm; the verb of Psalm 47:1.
Hebrew tsahal (H6670) — to cry shrilly, to shout for joy; used of Zion's rejoicing.
Greek keleusma (G2752) — a shouted command, an order given to troops or rowers; 1 Thessalonians 4:16.
Greek krazo (G2896) — to cry out, to shout; used of the crowds and of the demons.
usage: Of obedience made audible at Jericho: the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat (Joshua 6:20).
Of the shout commanded in worship: shout unto God with the voice of triumph (Psalm 47:1).
Of the Lord's own descending shout: the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city.
Ezra 3:11

And they sang together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the LORD; because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel. And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.
Psalm 47:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm for the sons of Korah. O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph.
1 Thessalonians 4:16
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:

pos: n. (in the KJV, a wind or pipe instrument; rendering Hebrew ugab)
etymology: From the Greek organon, an implement or instrument, through Latin organum. The Authorized Version uses it in the general old sense of a pipe or wind instrument; the church organ of later centuries takes its name from the same root but is not what the Hebrew ugab denotes.
biblical_def: The KJV organ renders Hebrew ugab, a pipe or wind instrument of some kind, and it appears only four times — but the four are placed with unusual care. It enters with the first culture: Jubal “was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ” (Genesis 4:21). That is in Cain's line, three verses before Lamech's boast of vengeance, and the placement is deliberate. Music is a gift of common grace that flourishes in a city under judgment; artistry is not evidence of righteousness. Job uses it twice, once of the prosperity of the wicked, whose children dance and who “rejoice at the sound of the organ” (Job 21:12), and once of his own reversal: “My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep” (Job 30:31). The same instrument serves feasting and lament; what changes is the man holding it. Finally the Psalter takes the instrument up into the worship of God without apology: “praise him with stringed instruments and organs” (Psalm 150:4). The arc is worth noticing. An instrument invented in the city of Cain, used by the prospering wicked and by a broken saint, ends the Psalter in the praise of God.
webster_summary: In the KJV a pipe or wind instrument (Hebrew ugab). It appears first in Cain's line, then in the mirth of the wicked and the mourning of Job, and last in the final psalm's call to praise God.
webster_full: ORGAN, n. [L. organum; Gr. organon, an instrument.] A natural instrument of action or operation; as the eye is the organ of vision.
2. The instrument or means of conveyance or communication; as, a newspaper is the organ of a party.
3. In music, the largest and most harmonious of wind instruments, consisting of pipes filled with wind and stops touched by the fingers.
4. In Scripture, a pipe or wind instrument; Jubal was the father of such as handle the harp and organ, Gen. 4.
5. Organ-pipe, the pipe of a musical organ.
corruption_summary: Instruments are made a test of party — one side treating them as worldly, another treating novelty as proof of life — while the KJV's organ is read anachronistically as the pipe organ of later church buildings.
corruption_paragraphs: Two smaller errors attach to this word. The first is anachronism: readers meet organ in Genesis 4 and picture the instrument of a Victorian chapel, which imports a whole controversy the text knows nothing of. Hebrew ugab is a pipe, probably a simple reed or flute; nothing in Scripture settles the later debate about what belongs in a meeting-house. The second error is to make instruments the frontier of faithfulness in either direction — to treat their absence as spirituality, or their novelty as vitality. The Psalter names instruments freely; the New Testament assembly is described without them. Prudence and the regulative principle govern the question, and it deserves less heat than it gets.

The principle to recover is the one Genesis 4:21 quietly teaches: skill in the arts is common grace, distributed without regard to the state of the soul. Jubal's line produced music and metalwork and also Lamech's song of vengeance. A gifted musician is a gifted musician, not thereby a godly man; and the church that selects its leaders in worship by talent alone has confused two different things. Job holds the balance — the same organ that sounded for the mirth of the wicked was turned in his hands to the voice of them that weep, and God was nearer in the second sound than in the first.
roots_summary: Hebrew ugab is a pipe or wind instrument, paired in Genesis with kinnor, the harp. Greek organon means simply an implement, from which the later musical sense narrowed.
roots_lines: Hebrew ugab (H5748) — a pipe or wind instrument; the KJV organ, in four places only.
Hebrew kinnor (H3658) — the harp or lyre, paired with the organ in Genesis 4:21.
Hebrew chalil (H2485) — a pipe or flute, bored through; used at feasts and in mourning.
Greek organon — an implement or tool of any kind; the general sense behind the English word.
Greek aulos (G836) — a pipe or flute; the New Testament instrument of piping, 1 Corinthians 14:7.
usage: Of the first musicians, in Cain's line: the father of all such as handle the harp and organ (Genesis 4:21).
Of the mirth of the prospering wicked: rejoice at the sound of the organ (Job 21:12).
Of an instrument turned to grief: my organ into the voice of them that weep (Job 30:31).
scriptures: Genesis 4:21
And his brother's name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.
They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ.
My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep.
Psalm 150:4
Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs.

pos: n. (an agreeable succession of sounds; sweet singing or playing; rendering Hebrew zimrah, Greek psallo in Ephesians 5:19)
etymology: From the Greek melodia, from melos, a song or tune, and ode, a song. The English has always meant the tune itself as distinct from the words or the harmony.
biblical_def: Melody in the Authorized Version is the sweetness of a tune, and Scripture judges it by what it accompanies. Isaiah gives it to a forgotten harlot city in bitter irony: “Take an harp, go about the city, thou harlot that hast been forgotten; make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered” (Isaiah 23:16). Beauty of sound is here a bid for attention by one who has nothing else left, and the prophet is not impressed. Amos gives the divine verdict on melody offered by the unjust: “I will not hear the melody of thy viols” (Amos 5:23). But the same word describes what God restores to a desolated people: he will make Zion's wilderness like Eden, so that there is found in her “joy and gladness… thanksgiving, and the voice of melody” (Isaiah 51:3). The decisive New Testament use relocates it: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19). The verb is psallo, originally to pluck a string, and Paul names the instrument — the heart. That is not a rejection of audible music but a statement of where the real music is made. A congregation may be in tune and silent in the heart, or plain in sound and full of melody where God hears.
webster_summary: An agreeable succession of sounds. Scripture rejects it from the unjust, restores it to a comforted Zion, and in Ephesians relocates it — melody made in the heart, to the Lord.
webster_full: MELODY, n. [Gr. melodia; melos, a song, and ode, ode.] An agreeable succession of sounds; a succession of sounds so regulated and modulated as to please the ear.
2. To constitute melody, the sounds must be arranged according to the laws of rhythmus, measure, or the due proportion of the movements.
3. Melody differs from harmony, as it consists in the agreeable succession of sounds; harmony consists in their agreeable union.
4. In Scripture, sweetness of sound; as, make sweet melody, Is. 23.
5. Making melody in the heart, Eph. 5; the inward praise of which the voice is the expression.
corruption_summary: Sweetness of sound is taken as evidence that worship has been accepted, though Amos records God refusing melody outright — while Ephesians 5:19 is used to excuse silence in the congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: The most common misuse runs through feeling: a service that sounded beautiful and moved the affections is assumed to have been received. Amos 5:23 forbids the inference. God there refuses melody from a people whose courts were corrupt, and the refusal is stated as a settled disposition, not a mood. Nothing about a tune can commend a worshipper whose dealings are false, and no amount of skill is a substitute for judgment running down as waters. The opposite abuse takes Paul's in your heart as permission to be silent, as though inward music excused a closed mouth. The same verse commands speaking to yourselves in psalms in its first clause; the heart is where the melody is made, not where it is hidden.

The principle to recover is Isaiah 51:3, which is the sweetest thing said about this word. God does not merely forgive a wasted people; he plants the waste places and puts the voice of melody back among them. That is the gospel order — comfort first, then thanksgiving, then singing. Melody is not the price of God's favour but one of its ordinary fruits, and a heart that has been made like a garden will not stay quiet for long.
roots_summary: Hebrew zimrah is melody or song of praise, from zamar, to make music. Greek psallo is to pluck a string, and so to sing praise; melos is the tune itself.
roots_lines: Hebrew zimrah (H2172) — melody, a song of praise; from zamar, to strike the strings.
Hebrew neginah (H5058) — a stringed instrument or the music of one; also a taunting song.
Greek psallo (G5567) — to pluck, to twang a string, and hence to sing praise; the verb of Ephesians 5:19.
Greek melos — a tune, a limb; the root of melody, distinct from harmony.
Greek kardia (G2588) — the heart; the instrument Paul names in Ephesians 5:19.
usage: Of melody as a bid for notice: make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered (Isaiah 23:16).
Of melody refused by God: I will not hear the melody of thy viols (Amos 5:23).
Of melody made in the heart: singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord (Ephesians 5:19).
scriptures: Isaiah 23:16
Take an harp, go about the city, thou harlot that hast been forgotten; make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered.
Amos 5:23
Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols.
Isaiah 51:3

For the LORD shall comfort Zion: he will comfort all her waste places; and he will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the LORD; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.
Ephesians 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;

pos: n. pl. (those who sound the trumpets, chiefly the priests in Israel; from Hebrew chatsotserah, a trumpet)
etymology: From trumpet, Old French trompette, a diminutive of trompe. In Israel the office was restricted: the silver trumpets of Numbers 10 were to be blown by the sons of Aaron, so a trumpeter was a priest before he was a musician.
biblical_def: The trumpeters of Scripture hold an office, and the office is priestly. The law is explicit: “the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow with the trumpets; and they shall be to you for an ordinance for ever throughout your generations” (Numbers 10:8). The silver trumpets summoned the assembly, signalled the breaking of camp, sounded the alarm in war, and were blown over the sacrifices — every one of them a call requiring the people to know what it meant and to move. At the dedication of the temple the trumpeters and the singers act together: “as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD” (2 Chronicles 5:13), and the cloud fills the house. They also stand at the making of a king: when Athaliah looked, “the king stood by a pillar, as the manner was, and the princes and the trumpeters by the king” (2 Kings 11:14), and the sound she heard was the end of her usurpation. Revelation names them in the great lament over Babylon: “the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee” (Revelation 18:22). When a civilisation falls under judgment, its music stops. The trumpeters are the last to be silenced and their silence is total.
webster_summary: Those who sound the trumpets — in Israel a priestly ordinance for ever. They summon the assembly, stand beside a crowned king, join the singers as the glory falls, and fall silent when Babylon is judged.
webster_full: TRUMPETER, n. One who sounds a trumpet.
2. One who proclaims, publishes or denounces; as, a trumpeter of another's praise.
3. A large bird of South America, so called from the sound it utters.
4. In Scripture, the priests appointed to blow the silver trumpets, Num. 10.
5. TRUMPET, n. A wind instrument of music, used chiefly in war and military exercises.
corruption_summary: The trumpet is treated as mere ceremony, its signalling function forgotten — and with it the fact that God appointed particular men to sound particular calls the people were bound to know and obey.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 10 is not decoration. The silver trumpets carried a code: one trumpet summoned the princes, two summoned the whole assembly, an alarm meant the camps on the east side were to move. A people who forgot the code could not obey it, and a trumpeter who improvised would have scattered the nation. That is the background to Paul's uncertain sound in 1 Corinthians 14:8 and it exposes a modern instinct — that what is sounded in God's house may be whatever moves the hearer. The office existed to make a fixed meaning audible, and it was restricted to the priests precisely because the meaning was not theirs to alter.

The principle to recover is that God assigns offices and does not leave them to volunteers. The trumpeters were named, the singers were enrolled by family, the porters had their gates. This is the same instinct the New Testament carries into the church, where elders and deacons are the two offices, elders are to be plural, and the qualifications are written down. An age impatient with appointed office and fond of platform is exactly the age that most needs Numbers 10:8, where blowing the trumpet is called an ordinance for ever and given to particular men by name.
roots_summary: Hebrew chatsotserah is the straight silver trumpet of Numbers 10; shophar is the curved ram's horn. Greek salpistes is a trumpeter, from salpinx, a trumpet.
roots_lines: Hebrew chatsotserah (H2689) — the silver trumpet, blown by the priests; the instrument of Numbers 10.
Hebrew shophar (H7782) — the ram's horn, sounded at Jericho, at the jubile, and in alarm.
Hebrew taqa (H8628) — to blow, to thrust, to strike; the verb of sounding a trumpet.
Greek salpistes (G4538) — a trumpeter; the word in Revelation 18:22.
Greek salpinx (G4536) — a trumpet; the trump of God at the last day.

Of trumpeters beside a crowned king: the princes and the trumpeters by the king (2 Kings 11:14).
Of music silenced in judgment: the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee (Revelation 18:22).

2 Chronicles 5:13

2 Kings 11:14

And when she looked, behold, the king stood by a pillar, as the manner was, and the princes and the trumpeters by the king, and all the people of the land rejoiced, and blew with trumpets: and Athaliah rent her clothes, and cried, Treason, Treason.
Revelation 18:22

And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee; and no craftsman, of whatsoever craft he be, shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee;

pos: n. and ppr. (moving the body in measured steps, chiefly in celebration; rendering Hebrew machol and karar, Greek choros)
etymology: From Old French danser, of uncertain and probably Germanic origin. Hebrew machol is a round dance, from a root meaning to whirl; the biblical picture is a circle of celebrants rather than a couple.
biblical_def: Scripture's dancing is almost always public, corporate, and tied to a specific deliverance. After the sea, “Miriam the prophetess… took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances” (Exodus 15:20) — women together, in response to a salvation just witnessed. When the ark came up to Jerusalem, “David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod” (2 Samuel 6:14). Two details govern that verse: it was before the LORD, and the king wore the plain linen of a priest rather than royal robes. Michal despised him for it and was judged; the dancing was not the offence, the contempt was. The Psalter commands it: “Let them praise his name in the dance” (Psalm 149:3). Ecclesiastes sets it under the seasons, “a time to mourn, and a time to dance” (Ecclesiastes 3:4), which forbids both the man who will never dance and the man who never mourns. And the parable of the prodigal makes it the sound of a father's joy: the elder brother, still in the field, “heard musick and dancing” (Luke 15:25) and would not go in. The dancing in that house is heaven's over one sinner that repenteth, and the resentful man hears it from outside.
webster_summary: Measured motion in celebration. In Scripture it is public and corporate, tied to deliverance — Miriam after the sea, David before the ark — and it is the sound of the father's house when a lost son comes home.
webster_full: DANCE, v.i. [Fr. danser.] Primarily, to leap or spring; hence, to leap or step with measured steps, regulated by a tune, sung or played on a musical instrument.
2. To leap and frisk about; to move nimbly or up and down.
3. DANCING, ppr. Leaping and stepping to the sound of the voice or of an instrument.
4. DANCING, n. The act of moving with measured steps to music; a customary expression of joy or triumph.
5. In Scripture, David danced before the ark; and the daughters of Israel went out with dances to meet Saul, 1 Sam. 18.
corruption_summary: Dancing is either forbidden outright as worldly, or imported into worship in forms Scripture never knew — private, sensual, and expressive of the self rather than of a deliverance God has wrought.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors face each other here and both mishandle the text. Some traditions have banned dancing altogether, which requires them to be uneasy about Miriam, embarrassed by David, and silent on Psalm 149:3. That is too high a price. Others cite David to justify whatever a modern service can be induced to do, ignoring how carefully the narrative specifies the occasion — the ark of God returning to its place — and the manner, a king stripped to a linen ephod so that nothing of his rank showed. Neither the ban nor the licence reckons with what the Bible actually describes: corporate, public, joyful motion in response to a particular act of God, of which Herodias's daughter dancing for a king's pleasure (Mark 6:22) is the plain and terrible opposite.

The principle to recover is in Michal's window. She saw her husband leaping and dancing before the LORD and despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:16), and the chapter ends with her barrenness. What God judged was not a failure of decorum but contempt for a man's undignified gladness over the presence of God. There is a kind of respectability that cannot bear to see joy, and Scripture is harder on it than on the excess it disapproves. The elder brother in Luke 15 is the same figure, standing in the field, listening to the music, and refusing to come in.
roots_summary: Hebrew machol is a round dance, from chul, to whirl; karar is to whirl about, used of David. Greek choros is a band of dancers, the word in Luke 15:25.

Hebrew karar (H3769) — to whirl, to dance; used of David before the ark.
Hebrew raqad (H7540) — to skip, to leap, to dance; a time to dance, Ecclesiastes 3:4.
Greek choros (G5525) — a band of dancers, a dance; the sound the elder brother heard.
Greek orcheomai (G3738) — to dance; used of the daughter of Herodias, Mark 6:22.

Of a king before the ark: David danced before the LORD with all his might (2 Samuel 6:14).
